title: A Real RAG Pipeline Over Your Documents

content.goal: Create a documents folder and drop in a few real text files.
content.why: RAG answers from YOUR data. Use documents you actually care about — notes, a handbook, an FAQ. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 11, section 11.1.)
content.verify: A docs/ folder exists with at least one .txt file containing a few paragraphs of real content you can later ask questions about.

content.goal: Load and CHUNK the documents. Add chunking to atlas.py.
content.why: Chunking is the underrated make-or-break step — split at natural boundaries, keep chunks a few hundred words, with a little overlap. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 11, section 11.3.)
content.verify: Running chunk() on your notes produces a list of coherent passages, each a few hundred characters, split at paragraph boundaries with slight overlap.
content.troubleshoot: If chunks are one giant blob, your file has no blank lines between paragraphs — add them, or lower the size. Too-big chunks dilute meaning; too-small chunks lose context.

content.goal: Build the index — chunk, embed, and store each chunk with its source metadata.
content.why: This is Phase One of RAG (indexing), done once and re-run whenever documents change. Keep metadata so you can cite the source. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 11, section 11.2.)
content.verify: It prints how many chunks were indexed. Each entry carries its text, its source file (metadata for citations), and its meaning-vector.

content.goal: Retrieve the most relevant chunks for a question.
content.why: Phase Two begins with retrieval: embed the question, find the closest chunks by meaning. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 11, section 11.2.)
content.code:
def retrieve(question, k=3):
    qv = embed(question)
    scored = [(cosine(qv, item["vector"]), item) for item in INDEX]
    scored.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True)
    return [item for _, item in scored[:k]]
content.verify: retrieve("your question here") returns the 3 chunks most relevant in meaning, each with its source. These are what will be placed on the model's desk.

content.goal: Augment and generate — answer USING ONLY the retrieved context, with a citation.
content.why: The grounding instruction turns a hallucination-prone model into a checkable one: use only the context, admit ignorance, cite the source. (Learned in Phase 9, Ch 11, section 11.4.)
content.code:
def rag_answer(question, k=3):
    chunks = retrieve(question, k)
    context = "\n\n".join(f"[{i+1}] (source: {c['source']})\n{c['text']}"
                          for i, c in enumerate(chunks))
    return ask([
        {"role": "system", "content":
         "Answer the question using ONLY the context below. "
         "If the answer is not in the context, say you don't know. "
         "Cite the [number] of the piece you used."},
        {"role": "user", "content": f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"},
    ])

print(rag_answer("<ask something answerable from your docs>"))
content.verify: ATLAS answers from your documents and cites a [number]. Ask something NOT in your docs — it should say it doesn't know, rather than inventing an answer. That honesty is the grounding instruction working.
content.troubleshoot: If it hallucinates, strengthen "ONLY the context" and confirm retrieval actually returned relevant chunks (print them). Retrieval quality caps answer quality.

content.goal: CHECKPOINT — ATLAS can chat with your documents.
content.why: This is the workhorse pattern of the whole field, running on your machine over your own data.
content.verify: All true — documents are chunked, embedded, and indexed with source metadata; retrieval finds relevant chunks by meaning; answers are grounded in the context and cited; unanswerable questions get an honest "I don't know." Next unit turns retrieval into a TOOL so the AGENT decides when to search (agentic RAG).
